Family Health

Henna for hair: colour, application and safety

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Henna can create a lasting warm hair colour, but results and tolerability vary. A clear ingredient list, a strand test and instructions for the actual product are more useful than a universal recipe or a promise of healthier hair.

What henna is and what it can change

Henna is made from Lawsonia inermis leaves and has a long history of use for hair colour and body decoration in parts of Africa and Asia. Pure henna creates an orange-red to reddish-brown stain. The result depends on the starting colour, previous treatments, hair condition and the formulation, so the same powder will not produce the same shade on every person.

Historical medicinal uses are a different matter from hair colouring. Claims about treating illness, digestive problems or reproductive conditions are not reasons to swallow henna or use it as a pregnancy remedy. For hair, the practical question is whether the product can provide a colour you like without an unacceptable reaction or change in texture. Natural origin does not guarantee a suitable result.

Colour and texture benefits are different from treating the scalp

Some people find their hair looks glossier or feels fuller after henna, while others find it dry or difficult to manage. These experiences can depend on the mix and hair condition. References to tannins, vitamin E, protein or antioxidants do not establish that applying the powder nourishes the follicle or prevents future greying. Covering grey strands changes their appearance; it does not switch natural pigment production back on.

Henna is also promoted as an antifungal treatment for dandruff, scalp infection or hair loss. Laboratory activity of a plant ingredient is not proof that a homemade paste treats those problems in people. Persistent flaking, sores, patchy loss or excessive shedding should be assessed so that care targets the cause. A cosmetic dye should not delay that assessment or be applied to an already inflamed scalp.

Read past the words natural, neutral and black

The ingredient list is more useful than a colour name. Natural henna generally refers to Lawsonia, while products called neutral henna may contain other plants, such as cassia. They do not necessarily behave like pure red henna. A product labelled black henna may be a plant blend or may contain added dyes, including paraphenylenediamine, known as PPD. The label alone cannot tell you which.

PPD can cause serious allergy, and a previous black-henna temporary tattoo can increase the risk of a later hair-dye reaction. Choose a clearly labelled product from a traceable supplier and avoid unknown mixtures. This does not mean every henna product contains contaminants or PPD. It means purity and composition should be checked rather than assumed from words such as herbal, organic or chemical-free.

Henna and indigo are separate plant dyes

Indigofera tinctoria supplies indigo, a different colouring ingredient from Lawsonia. Henna and indigo may be combined, or used in a planned sequence, to create darker brown or black-looking shades. The instructions depend on the particular formulation. Applying indigo after henna is one possible method, not a universal recipe for every product or hair type.

Do not assume that henna is always temporary while indigo is always permanent. Colour persistence and later correction depend on the hair and the mixture, and henna colour can be difficult to remove. Neither plant should be treated as a guaranteed hair-growth treatment. Tell a stylist about previous plant dyes before bleaching, perming or applying another colour, especially if you do not know what the earlier product contained.

Test and choose the timing before a full application

Read all instructions before mixing. Follow the product’s allergy-test directions before each use, even if you used it successfully before. A negative home test does not guarantee that a full application will be reaction-free. If you previously had a dye reaction, get professional advice about the ingredient involved rather than repeatedly testing suspected products on yourself.

A strand test serves a different purpose: it helps you see the likely shade and how your hair feels afterward. This is particularly useful with grey, bleached, chemically treated, dry or very porous hair. Do not apply dye to a scratched, sunburned or irritated scalp. Arrange enough time for preparation and rinsing, but do not extend the contact time simply because a recipe promises a stronger result overnight.

Set up a clean space and suitable equipment

Henna can stain skin, towels and surfaces. Wear gloves and old clothing, protect your shoulders with a towel and cover the work area. Have clips for separating the hair, an applicator brush, a suitable mixing bowl and utensil, water and a timer ready. Use a cap only if the product instructions call for one; keep plastic coverings away from children and the face.

Choose equipment compatible with the product. A washable glass or ceramic bowl can be practical, while plastic may stain. A blanket claim that every metal utensil ruins every henna mix is not a substitute for the manufacturer’s directions. Keep dye away from eyes and do not use scalp hair dye on eyelashes or eyebrows. Do not use a hair dryer or sit in strong sun to accelerate processing unless the product specifically directs an appropriate method.

Mix according to the formulation, not a universal kitchen recipe

Powdered henna is commonly mixed with liquid into a workable paste, but the quantity, water temperature, resting time and storage instructions vary. A one-cup recipe may be far too much or too little for your hair. Use the amounts given for the product and your hair length. Do not assume every paste should stand overnight, or that refrigeration makes any homemade mixture safe to keep indefinitely.

Recipes sometimes add lemon juice or apple cider vinegar, or replace water with coffee or black tea for a darker effect. Hibiscus, red tea and beetroot juice are proposed for redder tones. These additions do not guarantee a predictable shade and may irritate skin or alter the formulation. Filtered or distilled water is not universally required either. Avoid improvising acids, drinks or other products when the directions call for a simpler mixture.

Apply in sections and monitor how your scalp feels

Prepare clean or dry hair as specified by the product; instructions differ. Divide the hair into manageable sections, then apply the paste evenly with gloved hands or the supplied brush. Working methodically from one section to the next, including the crown and roots where appropriate, is more useful than applying extra product indiscriminately. Use clips to keep treated sections separate if needed.

Keep the mixture away from your face and eyes and wipe accidental skin contact promptly. Start a timer and follow the stated processing period. Four or five hours, an overnight application and added heat are not universal requirements. Burning, itching or feeling unwell is a reason to stop, not a sign that the colour is working. Remove the product and seek advice if a reaction occurs.

Rinse thoroughly and care for the hair afterward

At the recommended time, rinse carefully until the paste is removed, following the instructions about water temperature, shampoo and conditioner. Some formulations recommend waiting before the next shampoo, but a fixed twenty-four-hour no-shampoo rule does not apply to every product. If you suspect an allergic reaction, washing the dye out promptly with mild shampoo takes priority over preserving colour.

Handle wet hair gently and avoid forceful rubbing or very hot drying. If the hair feels dry, use a suitable conditioner and reassess whether this product suits you before repeating it. Dry or frizzy hair does not automatically rule henna out, but a strand test is particularly valuable. Do not keep reapplying dye to correct a disappointing result without considering the cumulative colour and effect on the hair.

Treat food-based masks as optional mixtures, not repair treatments

Common homemade additions include egg, yoghurt, shikakai, soaked fenugreek, amla, aloe vera and flaxseed paste. These ingredients have different properties and can introduce allergy, irritation, spoilage or unpredictable colour effects. An elaborate recipe with several cup measures is not evidence that the mixture is suitable for your scalp or able to repair damaged hair.

There is no need to combine all of them with henna. In particular, do not leave an egg or dairy mixture warm for hours or overnight and assume a plant powder preserves it. A formulated conditioner with clear directions is often simpler to evaluate. If you choose a hair product containing a botanical ingredient, judge that finished product rather than treating a list of traditional ingredients as a proven treatment.

Recognise irritation and allergy

A reaction can cause stinging, itch, a rash, swelling or blisters on the scalp, face or neck. Symptoms may develop after a delay, including over the next few days. Severe inflammation can damage skin and contribute to hair loss; it should not be dismissed as normal sensitivity. Stop using the product, wash it off and ask a pharmacist or clinician for advice about a mild reaction.

Seek medical help for persistent or worsening symptoms, extensive blistering or marked facial swelling. Trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, mouth or tongue, faintness or collapse requires emergency care. Keep the packaging and ingredient list to help identify the cause. A dermatologist can assess allergy; switching to another product called natural does not necessarily avoid the same ingredient.

Using hair colour during pregnancy

Available guidance generally finds little exposure from using hair dye correctly on an intact scalp, and henna-based colour can be an option. Pregnancy can still change how the hair responds. Follow precautions such as gloves, ventilation, the shortest instructed contact time and thorough rinsing. Some people choose to wait until after the first twelve weeks, but that is a preference discussed in guidance rather than proof that earlier use necessarily causes harm.

Check the complete product rather than relying on the henna name, and ask your maternity clinician if you have a particular concern or a history of reactions. Do not use henna internally or as a medicinal preparation. Whether pregnant or not, you can postpone colouring, choose a different approach or keep your natural colour if the process does not feel right for you.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Plant-based hair colour can still irritate skin or cause allergy.

Product directions and ingredient checks take priority over generic timing, heating or mixing recipes.

How BeMama can help

Choose the shade and routine you want, test the result on a strand, and keep the packaging in case you need help identifying a reaction.

When to seek help

Stop and wash off a dye that causes a reaction. Breathing difficulty, mouth or tongue swelling, faintness or collapse requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Henna changes colour, not the underlying cause of greying or hair loss.
  • Black henna is a label to investigate, not a single dependable formula.
  • Strand tests and allergy tests answer different questions.
  • Do not assume overnight contact or kitchen additives are required.

Frequently asked questions

Will henna stop my hair turning grey?

No. It can colour grey strands but has not been shown to restore natural pigment production. Claims about tannins preventing greying should not be treated as established.

Is it a treatment for dandruff or hair loss?

Not a proven substitute for diagnosis and treatment. Persistent flaking, scalp sores or significant shedding needs assessment rather than repeated dye application.

Is black henna always pure indigo?

No. Some products contain plant blends and others added dyes such as PPD. Check the full ingredient list and avoid unknown mixtures.

Is neutral henna the same plant without the colour?

Not necessarily. That name may refer to another plant, such as cassia, or a blend. Read the ingredients and test the effect on a strand.

Can a negative patch test guarantee safety?

No. It reduces uncertainty but cannot rule out a reaction during full use. Follow the product instructions and seek advice after any previous dye allergy.

Must I leave henna on overnight?

No. Use the processing time for your product. Longer contact, added heat or sleeping with dye on is not a universal way to improve the result.

Should I add lemon juice, coffee or beetroot?

Only if the product directions support the addition. These ingredients can change the mixture or irritate skin and do not guarantee a particular shade.

Can an egg-and-yoghurt mask prevent dryness?

There is no reliable universal recipe. Food mixtures can spoil and cause reactions; a suitable formulated conditioner and strand testing are simpler ways to assess care.

Should I avoid shampoo if my scalp starts burning?

No. Suspected reaction takes priority over colour. Wash the product out promptly with mild shampoo and seek advice, with emergency help for breathing trouble or mouth swelling.

Can I use henna hair colour while pregnant?

It can be an option when used correctly, but check every ingredient and follow exposure precautions. Discuss previous reactions or individual concerns with your maternity clinician.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
